summary: Adds two commands to IMAP, MOVE and UID MOVE, which move messages from one mailbox to another. Before this, clients had to copy messages and then delete the originals as separate steps.

plainLanguage.summary: Moving a letter from one folder to another in one step, instead of copying it and then throwing the old one away.

questions: how to move email messages with imap
what is the imap move command
what is the difference between imap move and copy
subtitle: One IMAP command that moves messages between mailboxes without the copy, flag and expunge dance.

tldr.problem: Base IMAP has no move command, so clients must COPY, STORE a deleted flag and EXPUNGE. That is not atomic, can leave messages in odd intermediate states, and can expunge other messages that were already flagged for deletion.
tldr.mechanism: The MOVE extension adds MOVE and UID MOVE. The server moves each message to the target mailbox, giving it a new UID, and removes the original, so the client sees it as one action.
tldr.outcome: Clients get a safer, simpler move, and servers can use efficient back-end moves. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 6851 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2013, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3501.

sections.title: Why IMAP Needs a Move Command
sections.content:
RFC 6851 defines an extension to IMAP (RFC 3501) that makes it easy to move messages from one mailbox to another. It adds a new MOVE command and extends the UID command so that UID MOVE works too.

The base IMAP specification has no move function. Clients have had to combine COPY, STORE and EXPUNGE to do this very common operation. A server advertises the extension by returning MOVE as a capability in response to the CAPABILITY command.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, to move a toy to another box you would make a copy and then throw the first one away. This gives you a way to just pick it up and put it in the other box.

sections.title: Problems with Copy, Store and Expunge
sections.content:
The RFC lists the shortcomings of the old three-step approach. Moving a message that way is not an atomic process, so an interruption can leave messages in intermediate states. Because several clients can open the same mailboxes at the same time, other clients can see those intermediate states even without interruptions.

There is a side effect too: if the source mailbox holds other messages already flagged for deletion, the final expunge step can remove more than just the moved messages. Finally, servers with certain back-end message stores may have efficient ways to move messages without copying any data, and the copy-and-delete sequence cannot use them.
sections.plainLanguage: Copy-then-delete is like photocopying a page and then tearing out the original. If someone walks in halfway, they see two pages, and you might tear out the wrong ones.

sections.title: How MOVE and UID MOVE Work
sections.content:
MOVE takes two arguments: a message set and a mailbox name. For MOVE the set holds sequence numbers, and for UID MOVE it holds UIDs. Each message in the set is moved from the selected (source) mailbox to the named (target) mailbox. A new message with a new UID is created in the target, the original is removed from the source, and the client sees it as a single action. The result is OK if the move completed, NO if the messages cannot be moved or cannot go to that name, and BAD if the command is unknown or its arguments invalid.

The effect per message matches [UID] COPY, then [UID] STORE +FLAGS.SILENT \DELETED, then UID EXPUNGE, but the semantics are not identical. The intermediate states do not occur, and the server MUST NOT generate STORE response codes or set the \DELETED flag on any message. COPY and EXPUNGE response codes are still returned.

Because a move covers a set, it may fail partway. Each message SHOULD either be moved or left alone. The server MUST leave every message in at least one of the two mailboxes, so nothing is lost, and SHOULD NOT leave any message in both. This holds even when the server returns a tagged NO.

Extensions that affect COPY affect MOVE in the same way, so response codes such as TRYCREATE are sent as appropriate. Moving to the currently selected mailbox is allowed when copying there is allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the server which messages and which folder. It puts each one in the new folder and removes it from the old one, and it promises no message ever ends up lost.

sections.title: Example and Pipelining Cautions
sections.content:
The RFC gives this exchange, in which the server sends a COPYUID code, then a series of EXPUNGE responses, then the tagged OK. The server may also send unrelated EXPUNGE responses if other messages happen to be expunged at the same time, which is normal IMAP operation.

The server may send EXPUNGE (or VANISHED) responses before the tagged response. A client therefore cannot safely send more commands with message sequence number arguments while the server is processing a move. Both commands can be pipelined with other commands, but care is needed, because the renumbering that follows an EXPUNGE makes it unsafe to pipeline any command that relies on sequence numbers after a move. Likewise, a move cannot be pipelined with a command that might cause renumbering.

Implementers need to read RFC 4315 to understand UID EXPUNGE, though full implementation of it is not necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: While the server is tidying up, the numbering of the messages in the folder can shift. So the client should not point at messages by position until the server says it is done.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Extensions
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC covers how MOVE works alongside other IMAP extensions.

  • QUOTA (RFC 2087): a MOVE may succeed where a COPY would cause a quota overrun.
  • ACL (RFC 4314): the rights required are the union of those for UID STORE, UID COPY and UID EXPUNGE.
  • UIDPLUS (RFC 4315): servers SHOULD send COPYUID in response to UID MOVE, and are advised to send it in an untagged OK before the EXPUNGE or moved responses, so clients do not see an expunge before the matching COPYUID.
  • QRESYNC (RFC 5162): the server SHOULD send VANISHED rather than EXPUNGE, as for UID EXPUNGE, and the client must handle both. A server that stores modification sequences MUST increment the per-mailbox mod-sequence when messages are moved, send HIGHESTMODSEQ, and give moved messages new mod-sequences higher than the highest in the target mailbox.
  • Sieve events (RFC 6785): MOVE is treated like COPY, so a script can be invoked with imap.cause set to COPY, but never FLAG, because MOVE does not change flags.
sections.plainLanguage: MOVE is meant to play nicely with the other add-on features of IMAP, such as storage limits, permissions and keeping a client in sync.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The RFC defines the syntax in ABNF. It adds MOVE to the list of capabilities and to the commands usable once a mailbox is selected, and it adds move as an allowed argument of UID. The command is MOVE, a space, a sequence set, a space and a mailbox name. Token strings are case insensitive and implementations MUST accept them that way.
sections.plainLanguage: The grammar just says what a MOVE line looks like: the word MOVE, which messages, and where to.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
MOVE adds no new capabilities to IMAP, which limits its security impact. Its transactional semantics may still interact with implementations in unexpected ways. For example, moving messages between mailboxes under the quota root may require temporary suspension of quota checking. Different mailboxes may also have different antispam, antivirus or auditing policies, and messages may need rescanning with updated rules after a move.

On the positive side, MOVE removes the need for complicated client algorithms to handle partial failures of the STORE, COPY and EXPUNGE trio, and incomplete versions of those algorithms can lead to mail loss. IANA added MOVE to the IMAP 4 Capabilities registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving mail is safer than the old way, but the server has to make sure its spam and virus checks still apply in the new folder.
